steps.text: Are you going to wait too? Oh, please wait. There's a cliff path all the way round. It's the most beautiful walk in Saltmere.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: We could all go. Well — Fenn won't. He'll sit here and look at the sea like it owes him money. But we could.
Zizzy hesitates. Seven hours. She'd meant to oil the chain, re-read the map, plan tomorrow to the minute. Be useful.
Pony says nothing. But he's looking at the cliff path the way he looks at a plaque.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …Fine.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Yay!
The cliff path is everything Clover promised. A ribbon of sheep-cropped turf along the clifftops, sea pinks nodding in clumps.
Far below, the sea breaks white on black rock and pulls back, endlessly patient.
Pony falls behind at once. There's a plaque about seabirds. A second about a smuggler called Black Annie. An interesting rock.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Go on! I'll catch up! There's a — this rock has a fossil in it!

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's a rock!

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's a rock with a *fossil* in it!
So it's Zizzy and Clover, side by side, along the top of the world.
Clover talks the way some people breathe. Her sister, who has four children. Her job at a garden centre, in charge of the succulents, which she treats like grandchildren.
How she first rode the Long Way Round at seventeen, on a dare, and has come back every year since.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: The first year the Hat gave me Fenn, I thought he hated me. He didn't say one word to me for two whole days.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Not one. So I thought, right, I'll talk enough for both of us.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: That sounds like a lot of talking.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: It was! Then on day three we were stuck on the Spit waiting for the tide, and I was talking about my sister's wedding.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: And he said, out of nowhere, "Did the cake fall over?" I'd told him about the cake on day one.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: He'd remembered *everything*. He'd just been listening.
She smiles out at the sea.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Some people listen with their whole body. You just have to learn what it looks like.
Zizzy glances back. Far behind, a small figure in a black beanie crouches over a rock, the wind tugging his scarf.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: He reads everything. Plaques. Posters. Shampoo bottles.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: And you?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: What about me?

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: What do you do with your whole body?
Zizzy doesn't answer straight away. She holds her hat down against the wind.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Fence. I used to fence.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Oh! Swords! Like his little wooden one?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Not like his little wooden one.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: "Used to"?
There it is. The gap in the guard. Clover doesn't lunge at it. She notices it, stops, and looks at it kindly.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I'm busy now.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Okay.
Just like Pony. Zizzy is starting to suspect the whole island chain is in a conspiracy not to push her.
They walk on. Two choughs tumble past below the cliff edge, red-legged and shrieking.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: I'm going to beat you, you know. I really want to.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: I came second twice, both times behind Fenn, when he was riding with someone else. Then the Hat gave me him.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: He says I'm the reason we'll win. I don't think he believes it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You've never won.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Never! Fenn's the champion. I'm "Fenn's partner". It's fine. It's fine!

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: I'd just like — once — for them to read my name off the plaque first.
For the first time there's something under Clover's sunshine. Not a cloud. Just weather. Zizzy knows it. She's carrying her own.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Then you'd better ride fast.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: I always ride fast.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: So do I.
Clover bumps her shoulder. Zizzy, who doesn't do shoulder bumps, finds she's allowed it.
Pony catches up near Keeper's Point, out of breath, pink-nosed, holding a small grey stone the size of a coin.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Ammonite. Look at it. A hundred and eighty million years old.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Older than the cliff. Older than the *sea*, probably, this bit of it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's a snail.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's a *cephalopod*. It's a tiny spiral of time. It's — here.
He holds it out to her. Just like that. As if it's obvious.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: What?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You keep it. For — I don't know. For luck.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You don't have anything lucky. Everybody should have something lucky on a race.
The little ridged spiral curls inward, like a staircase going somewhere very small and very old.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You have a sword.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: The sword's not for luck.
She waits for him to say what it *is* for. He doesn't. He holds out the stone.
She takes it. It's warm from his hand. She puts it in her shirt pocket, over her heart, without thinking.
By the time she thinks, it's too late to move it without being obvious.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.expr_raw: very quietly, to the sea, delighted
steps.text: Oh, no.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: What.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Nothing! Choughs. Lovely choughs.
At half past four the whole field sits on the black rocks below Keeper's Point like seals.
The eleven o'clock crowd are back, sunburned and grumpy. All they found was seaweed and a crab.
The tide pulls back. And back. Further than seems possible, uncovering a long shelf of weed-dark rock and pools glittering like dropped mirrors.
At the very end, half-buried in barnacles, a green bronze ship's bell lies on its side.
Tied to its clapper, in a plastic bag against the sea: a rubber stamp and a stack of folded paper.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Go.
It's not a race, exactly. It's not *not* a race. Forty-odd cyclists scramble over wet rock in cleats.
Somebody slips into a rock pool up to the waist. Clover hauls them out, laughing.
Fenn doesn't run. He walks. Somehow he's still the second one there.
The first is Zizzy, who has never in her life walked when she could lunge.
She stamps the passport — a little bell, carved in surprising detail into a potato that has clearly been through a lot — and takes a riddle.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: What does it say?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: "*Where the trees wear red and the green is crowned, where the hands are blistered and the band goes round —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: come to the queen of the summer fair, and find what was lost by what is there.*"

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Sorrel Isle. Orchards. Apple fête. They crown an Apple Queen every year.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It was on the ferry office noticeboard.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Of course you did.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: "Find what was lost by what is there." That's not the destination. That's the clue *at* the destination.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I don't know what it means yet.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: Tomorrow.
He's reading the same riddle off his own slip, unbothered.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: You'll know when you see it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Do you know?

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: I've been to the fête.
That's all. He tucks the slip in his hoodie pocket and heads back across the rocks.
The Gullrock campsite is a sloping field behind the lighthouse, tents in the lee of an old stone wall. Giraffy's big pot is going. Bruno's van has its back doors open and the saxophone on.
Tent forty-one is the smallest, last in the row, next to a gorse bush. Pony eyes it with deep suspicion.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Don't worry, strawberry. I've had a word with it.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Thank you.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: It says it's very sorry about your tyre and it'd like to take you out for a drink.
Dinner is fish stew. Giraffy says it's different. This time it actually is. Over the bowls, Clover leans across, eyes shining.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Tonight's the night, if you want. The cove on the north side. You can only reach it after the tide turns.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: The water's warm. It's shallow and it's been in the sun all day.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: And if it's a dark night and the water's still, it glows. Little lights. When you move.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Bioluminescence. Plankton. *Noctiluca scintillans*.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Yes! Him! What he said! Come with us, both of you. It's the best thing on the whole race.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Fenn's even coming, and Fenn doesn't come to anything.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: I'm going to sit on a rock.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: He's going to sit on a rock. Very supportively.
Beside her, Pony goes very still. His spoon has stopped halfway to his mouth.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Sure.
She says it before she's decided, watching his ears pin flat under the beanie, the way they did on the first day with the whole quay staring.
The cove is a horseshoe of pale sand in black rock, the water inside so still it looks like poured glass.
The moon isn't up yet. Stars go all the way down to the water.
Clover goes in first, shrieking at the temperature even though it's warm, and floats on her back laughing.
Every time she moves her hands, the water flares with tiny blue-green sparks, like someone stirring a bowl of stars.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Oh! Oh, it's *on*! Come in! Come *in*!
Fenn sits on a rock, as promised, hood up, watching her with an expression that, on a less guarded face, would be called fond.
Zizzy pulls off her shirt — swimsuit underneath; she planned for this, as she plans for everything — and folds it onto a rock. The hat goes on top.
The ammonite in the pocket clicks softly against the stone.
Pony stands at the very edge of the water. Fully dressed. Beanie on.
He holds the wooden sword in both hands, like someone at a bus stop holding an umbrella against rain that might come.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You said you swim.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I said I swim in the general sense.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: What's the specific sense?
A long pause. The sea laps at the toes of his boots.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I can't. Not really. I can sort of stay up. For a bit. If I don't think about it.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: And then I think about it.
He laughs, short, embarrassed.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I had lessons when I was seven. I stopped after three weeks. I was scared of the deep end.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Mum said I could try again next year. I never did. It's the first thing I remember quitting.
He turns the sword over in his hands. Where a wave breaks at his feet, the sea sparks faintly.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: That's stupid, isn't it. It's a swimming lesson. It's not a big thing.
Zizzy looks at him: beanie, sword, scarf, and the way he's standing, braced, as if he expects the sea to say something cruel.
She thinks of her grandmother at the rail. Going anyway.

options.label: "Come on. I've got you." Teach him.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's not stupid.
She holds out her hand.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's shallow. It's warm. I'm a strong swimmer. I've got you.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You — what if I —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You won't. Because I won't let you. That's the rule.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Whose rule?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Mine. It's new.
He looks at her hand for a long moment. Then he lays the sword carefully on the sand. Glasses off, folded, on top of the sword.
The beanie last, slowly, like it costs something. On top of the glasses.
And takes her hand.
They wade in together. Warm as a bath: knees, waist, chest. Every step spills blue light across the cove.
He's shaking. She can feel it through his fingers.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Lie back.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: That sounds like a terrible idea.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Lie back. I'll hold you. Look up.
He lies back. Her hands are under his shoulders, flat and steady, the way she'd hold a blade level. He's rigid as a plank.
Then, slowly, the water takes him. His ears come up. His tail floats out behind him, sparkling. Stars above. Stars in the water all around.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Oh.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: See?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'm floating. I'm — I'm actually —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You are.
She eases her hands. Not away. Just less. He doesn't notice. He's watching light pour off his own fingers.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's like being inside the sky.
No glasses, no beanie, wet hair spread pale gold on the dark water.
He looks happy. Simply happy, in a way she hasn't seen anyone look since March.
She's been holding him up for two minutes. For two minutes she hasn't thought about the lease once.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …I've barely got you, you know.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You're mostly doing it yourself.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Don't tell me that. I'll think about it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Then don't think about it.
He doesn't. They stay in the warm dark until the moon comes up. On his rock, Fenn watches. In the water, Clover very carefully swims the other way to give them room.

options.label: "So you're a horse who can't swim. Seahorses everywhere are ashamed." Tease him in.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: So you're a horse who can't swim. Seahorses everywhere are ashamed.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: That's — that's not even the same animal!

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: They'd still be ashamed. They'd write letters.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Seahorses can't write!

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Not with that attitude.
He laughs properly, the bright startled laugh like the duck bell, and his shoulders come down from round his ears.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.expr_raw: wading in to her knees, turning back
steps.text: It's up to my knees. Come and stand.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.expr_raw: wading in to her knees, turning back
steps.text: Standing isn't swimming. Standing is just a bath with a view.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: …Just standing.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You can stand there and tell me facts about plankton. You'd love that.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I would love that.
He takes the beanie off and puts it on the sword. Wades in, wincing: knees, then waist. The water lights up round him. He gasps.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Oh — *oh* —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Plankton facts. Go.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Okay, so *Noctiluca* means "night light". They glow when they're disturbed. It's a defence mechanism.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: So technically we're *scaring* them, which is awful, but also —
He talks for twenty minutes, waist-deep in starlight, waving his arms to make the water glow. He doesn't notice he's drifted out to where his feet barely touch.
Zizzy notices. She stays close. She doesn't tell him.

options.label: "You don't have to." Sit with him on the sand instead.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You don't have to.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: But you came all this way —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: The water'll be here. The plankton'll be here.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: They're not going anywhere. They don't have legs.
She sits on the cool sand beside his boots. After a moment he sits too, the sword across his knees.
They watch Clover sparkle and splash. They watch Fenn watch Clover. The tide breathes in and out at their feet, throwing up sparks.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Thank you.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: For what?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Not making me.
She doesn't answer. She skims a pebble flat across the glassy water. Four skips, each leaving a ring of blue light.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: How did you —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Wrist. Flat. Low.
He throws. It goes straight down with a plop and a single sad spark.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I think I've drowned it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: At least one of you went in.
He laughs. They stay till the moon comes up, skipping stones, his slightly less terrible each time.
They walk back over the headland by torchlight, sand in their shoes. Clover and Fenn walk ahead, her wet hair dripping down her trench coat.
Fenn has given her his hoodie. He walks in a T-shirt, hands in his pockets, pretending he's not cold.
Pony walks beside Zizzy, beanie back on, sword over his shoulder, very quiet.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Zizzy?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Mm.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You didn't laugh. When I told you. About the lessons.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It wasn't funny.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Most people would've. A bit. Not cruelly.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Just, "Aw, you can't swim." Like it's sweet.
She thinks about it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: My grandmother was scared of boats. She went on them every summer anyway.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Gripped the rail the whole way and said *allez* through her teeth, like she was going into a bout.
She doesn't know why she says it. It's the third thing she's told him about her grandmother. That's three more than she's told anyone.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: That's brave.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: She'd say it isn't brave if you're not scared. It's just going on a boat.
They walk on. The lighthouse beam swings over them, slow and steady: the path, the field, the sea, the path again.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: She sounds like someone I'd have liked.
Zizzy doesn't answer. She closes her hand round the ammonite in her pocket and keeps it there all the way back to the tent.
That night, through the divider, she hears him whisper, half asleep:

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Night lights. *Noctiluca*. Thank you for tonight, Zizzy.
She doesn't answer. But she falls asleep with the stone in her hand.
Sorrel Isle smells of apples from the moment the ramp goes down. Apples, cut grass, frying onions, and under it, faintly, the sea.
The island is low and green, laced with orchards. Every lane is roofed with branches heavy with red fruit. Windfalls lie in the road like dropped marbles.
A wasp follows Pony for a quarter of a mile in what he calls "a very personal way".
The fête is on the green at Hollin, ringed with bunting, apple crates and striped stalls.
There's a brass band — the same one from Port Amble, which follows the race round the islands "for the cider" — a coconut shy, a tug-of-war rope, a tea tent, a cake table groaning with pies.
At the far end, under a canopy of woven willow, stands an empty wooden throne heaped with apples.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: The Apple Queen's throne.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's a chair with fruit on.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's a *ceremonial* chair with fruit on. They crown her at sunset. There's a dance after.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's been going since 1740-something.
She holds the tandem by its handlebars and looks at the crowd. Apple-red children running between stalls. Old couples in deckchairs. A dog in a bow tie.
It's loud and bright and happy, and it makes the well inside her feel deeper, not shallower.

Fêtes were her grandmother's favourite thing. Every summer she ran a fencing demonstration at the one back home: children queuing to hold a foil for the first time, faces going solemn under the masks.
Zizzy hasn't been to a fête since.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Riddle?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Riddle.
She takes it out of the passport and reads it again.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: "*Come to the queen of the summer fair, and find what was lost by what is there.*"

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Okay. The queen of the fair is the throne. So what's by the throne?
Beside the willow canopy, a small white tent with a hand-painted sign: LOST & FOUND.
Inside, a very old ewe in a straw hat sits behind a table of single gloves, lone sandals, a child's red umbrella, false teeth in a jam jar, and one small rubber stamp.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Hello. We're with the race. Forty-one. Can we have the stamp?

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ewe
steps.text: Ooh, no, dear. It's lost property.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ewe
steps.text: You can only take something if you bring something.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Bring what?

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ewe
steps.text: Something lost! Find something somebody's lost, bring it here, and then you can have what's there.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ewe
steps.text: That's the rule. The lady with the glasses was very particular. She wrote it on a card.
She holds up a laminated card in Pia's bold, looping hand: *Find what was lost. Bring it home. — P.*

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …Pia.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: That's lovely, though. Isn't it lovely?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's a riddle that makes you be nice to strangers.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's a riddle that makes you search a field.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Those aren't opposites.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: If you say that one more time this week —

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You'll what?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …I'll think of something.
Forty teams search the fête for lost things. It's chaos.
Someone brings in a cat that isn't lost, just walking. Someone brings the vicar's reading glasses, which were on his head.
Clover finds a lost teddy bear in under ten minutes and gives it straight back to a sobbing toddler.
Only afterwards does she remember the stamp, and go back to ask, very apologetically, to borrow it for one minute.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: I forgot it was a *race*! He was so sad! Look at his little face!
Fenn has already found a car key in the grass by the tug-of-war rope, without seeming to look. He hands it in, takes the stamp, and goes to stand under a tree.
Zizzy searches methodically, row by row, under every stall. She finds a bottle cap, a crisp packet and a great deal of grass.
She straightens up from under the jam stall and sees Pony across the green, crouched beside a small lamb in dungarees who is crying the furious, gulping cry of the very young and very wronged.
She walks over.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: — and what colour was it?

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Lamb
steps.text: R-red.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Red. Good. That's very helpful. Red's easy to see.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: And when did you last have it?

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Lamb
steps.text: At the — the knight.
Pony looks up. At the edge of the green there's a stall painted like a castle: BEAT THE KNIGHT! THREE TOUCHES WINS A PRIZE!
In front of it, a life-size wooden knight on a spring, holding a padded sword, bobs in the breeze.
And beside the knight, in the grass, a small red mitten.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Found it.
He fetches it, kneels again, and puts it on the lamb's hoof himself, tucking the cuff in.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: There. Don't take it off again unless you really have to, okay?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Things get lost so easily when you're having fun.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Lamb
steps.text: Okay.
The lamb runs off. Pony turns round and finds Zizzy right there, watching.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Oh. Hi. I didn't — we needed it for the stamp, didn't we.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I gave it back. I didn't think.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: No. You didn't.
She doesn't sound angry. That's what throws him. He can't read what she does sound like, under the hat.
Something has gone soft and stupid in her chest, watching him tuck a mitten into a cuff. She has no idea where to put it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: We'll find something else.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Really? You're not —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: We'll find something else.
Forty minutes later, they do: a child's blue sandal, wedged under the coconut shy. Zizzy finds it. She very nearly smiles in public.
The ewe tuts kindly and stamps their passport: an apple, slightly bruised, carved into a potato by Giraffy at what must have been two in the morning.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ewe
steps.text: There you are, dears. Four stamps.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ewe
steps.text: The lady says your next riddle comes tonight at the crowning. And tomorrow's a rest day, so don't rush.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: A rest day?

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ewe
steps.text: Every year. She says even riddles need a nap.
Zizzy stares at the passport. A whole day of not riding, not winning, not being useful. Nothing to keep her mind off — anything.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You look like someone just told you you've been sentenced to a holiday.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I have.
They walk the fête till sunset. Pony buys two toffee apples and hands her one without asking. She eats it the way she eats everything: efficiently, pretending not to enjoy it.
They pass the BEAT THE KNIGHT stall again. The stallholder, an old ram with a magnificent moustache, leans on the counter, bored.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ram
steps.text: Three touches, young sir! Win the lady a prize!

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I'm not a lady. I'm a captain.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ram
steps.text: Win the captain a prize!
Pony looks at the wooden knight. At the padded sword on the counter. At the sword on his own back.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: …Can I use my own?

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ram
steps.text: Is it wood?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Beech.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ram
steps.text: Then it's a fair fight. Fifty pence.
Pony pays. Steps to the chalk line. Draws the wooden sword.
And something changes.
It's like watching someone take off a coat. The fidgeting stops. His shoulders come down and back.
His feet find a line — front foot at the knight, back foot at a right angle, knees soft. His free hand lifts behind him, light and curved.
The sword comes up into a guard: narrow, quiet, *correct*.
Zizzy goes very still.
She knows that stance the way she knows her own handwriting. Not just fencing. The old French school: upright, elegant, a little old-fashioned.
The way her grandmother taught it. The way almost nobody teaches it any more.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: *En garde*.
The ram pulls a lever. The knight springs forward, swinging.
Pony parries — a neat little circle of the blade — and touches the knight's chest. *Tok.*
It swings back. He gives half a step, lets it come, parries, touches. *Tok.*
The third time it comes fast and low, and Pony doesn't parry at all. He simply isn't where it thinks he is. His blade rests on the knight's wooden neck.
*Tok.*

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Ram
steps.text: Well, I'll be.
A little crowd has gathered. Someone claps. Pony comes back to himself all at once, like waking, and goes bright pink under the beanie.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Sorry. I mean — thank you.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's a very good knight. It's very — wooden.
The prize is a small, hideous china horse with a gold-painted mane. Pony stares at it with deep emotion.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's me.
He turns round with it. Zizzy is right there, closer than before, looking at him the way she looks at a map she can't read.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Who taught you that.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: What?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: The guard. The circle parry. The retreat on the third. That's not a club.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Nobody teaches it like that any more. Who taught you?
Pony's face does something complicated. Not a lie forming. A door, half open, while he decides whether to open it the rest of the way.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: A teacher. Once. A long time ago.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Where?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.expr_raw: soft, looking down at the china horse
steps.text: A summer class. In a town I never went back to.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.expr_raw: soft, looking down at the china horse
steps.text: I was nine. I only went for a fortnight. Then we moved.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: A fortnight? You learned *that* in a fortnight?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: No. I learned it in ten years. She just showed me where to start.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Then I kept going. On my own. In the back garden, mostly. Against a washing line.
Ten years. A washing line. In a year full of quitting, the one thing he never put down.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: And the sword?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: She gave it to me. On the last day. Said I had good feet.
Zizzy opens her mouth. She has a name in her head she hasn't said aloud since March, and the question would be so easy.
But the crowd is still there. The ram is saying "Another go, young sir?" And Pony has turned away, pink, to show the china horse to Clover, who coos at it.
The moment closes. Zizzy lets it. There's no point, she tells herself. Lots of people teach the old school. Probably.
She finds the ammonite in her pocket. Holds it.
Late afternoon, she finds Giraffy behind the tea tent, peeling apples into a bucket, one long unbroken spiral after another. He doesn't look up.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Sit, if you like.
She sits on a crate. Neither of them speaks. Peel drops into the bucket. On the green, the band starts and stops a song three times.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: How do you do it in one piece?

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Slowly. Most people go fast and it breaks.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Then they start again and go faster, because they're cross. Then it breaks again.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Is this a metaphor.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: It's an apple. But it can be a metaphor if you need one.
He hands her the knife and an apple. She peels fast and neat. It breaks after three turns.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Again.
Again. Slower. Five turns. Again. Seven. On the fourth apple the long red spiral drops into the bucket whole, and she's absurdly pleased.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: There.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: My grandmother used to say "again" like that.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Good word. Doesn't get enough credit.
He takes the knife back and goes on peeling. He doesn't ask about her grandmother. He doesn't say anything for a while.
In the apple-smelling shade, with a giraffe who asks for nothing, the well inside her is just still water. For ten minutes.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: He's looking for you, by the way. The horse.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Has been for a bit.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I wasn't hiding.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: I didn't say you were.
At sunset the village gathers round the willow throne. Fairy lights come on in the apple trees.
The band, loosened by cider, plays something that's a march or a waltz, depending which side of it you're on.
The Apple Queen is crowned: a hen of ninety-one, queen eleven times, who treats the whole thing as a formality.
She's handed a crown of apple blossom and a mug of cider, and looks happier with the cider.
Pia climbs onto a hay bale with a stack of envelopes, sees forty expectant faces, freezes, and starts handing envelopes to the nearest people to pass along, like exam papers.

steps.speaker: pia
steps.text: Sorry. Pass them on. Thank you. Sorry.
Envelope forty-one reaches them via a weasel, two badgers and a startled vicar. Inside, in Pia's bold, looping hand:
*"Rest. Then cross where the sea forgets the road twice a day, and remember it twice a night. Bring your courage. Bring a coat. — P."*

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: The Spit. The tidal causeway. "Forgets the road twice a day" — it floods at high tide.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: "Bring a coat." In August.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Everything's on purpose with Pia.
Zizzy thinks of her purple coat, folded at the bottom of the pannier. The one she couldn't leave behind.
The band strikes up properly. The green fills with couples. The Apple Queen dances with the vicar, crown wobbling.
Zizzy stands at the edge with a riddle in her hand and a horse beside her who is suddenly, visibly, very nervous.
Before anything else can happen, she turns to him. His collar is wrong.
It's been wrong all day, the mustard shirt buttoned one off so one side sticks up like a wing. She can't ignore it for one more second.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Hold still.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: What — why —
She undoes the top two buttons and does them up properly, quick and neat. Then she flattens the collar with both hands, one side, then the other.
Her fingers rest for a second at the sides of his neck, where the cream-tan fur is warm.
The first time she's touched him on purpose. Not to steady the bike. Not because a mechanic dared her. Just because his collar was wrong and she wanted it right.
She takes her hands away. Neither of them mentions it.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: …Thank you.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It was annoying me.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Since when?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Since nine this morning.

steps.prompt: The band starts a slow tune. Couples drift onto the green.

options.label: Ask him.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Do you dance?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Do I — in the general sense?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: In the specific sense. Now. Here.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I — yes? Badly. Very badly. I'm a hazard. There should be a sign.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Then I'll steer.
He looks at her hand for a long moment. Then he takes it.

options.label: Wait and let him ask.

steps.text: She doesn't ask. She waits, hands behind her back, watching the dancers, saying nothing. For Zizzy, that's the loudest thing she can do.

then.text: Beside her, he takes a breath. Pushes his glasses up. Another breath. She feels him gather himself, the way he did at the chalk line.

then.speaker: pony
then.text: Zizzy. Would you dance with me?
No joke. No ramble. Just the question, plainly, like a blade offered hilt-first.

then.speaker: zizzy
then.expr_raw: soft, before she can stop it
then.text: Yes.
It surprises them both.

else.text: Beside her, he takes a breath. Pushes his glasses up. Opens his mouth.

else.speaker: pony
else.text: Do you — think the Apple Queen's having a nice time?

else.speaker: zizzy
else.text: …Yes.

else.speaker: pony
else.text: Okay. Good. Great. That's — great for her.
He breathes. Tries again.

else.speaker: pony
else.text: Would you — like a toffee apple — no, you've had a toffee apple —

else.speaker: pony
else.text: would you like to — dance? With — me? Ideally?

else.speaker: zizzy
else.expr_raw: biting back something that is definitely not a smile
else.text: Ideally.

else.speaker: pony
else.text: Is that a yes?

else.speaker: zizzy
else.text: It's a yes. It took you three tries.

else.speaker: pony
else.text: I'm a "catching up later" person.

options.label: Clover is standing alone at the edge of the green. Ask her instead.

steps.text: Across the green, Clover stands alone at the edge of the lights. Fenn is under his tree. Not dancing, not looking, not leaving.
Clover is pretending not to mind. Her ears have drooped, just slightly.
Zizzy walks over before she can think about it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Dance.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: With *you*?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You talk enough for both of us. I'll lead enough for both of us.
Clover laughs and grabs her hand. They're terrible together. Clover dances like a bouncing ball. Zizzy dances like a fencing drill.
Halfway through, Clover is laughing so hard she has to stop.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Thank you. I needed that. He doesn't dance. He never has.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: I keep thinking one year he will.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: He's watching.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: He always watches. That's the thing.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: It's never enough, and it's never nothing.
Across the green, Pony stands holding a china horse, watching Zizzy laugh — the door-creak — with somebody else.
He looks happy about it. And a tiny bit like someone outside a lit window.
When the song ends, she walks back without a word, takes the china horse out of his hands, puts it in the tandem's basket, and holds out her hand.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: One. Then bed.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: One.
They dance under the apple trees, on grass soft with windfalls. He's terrible. He steps on her foot twice and apologises four times.
He holds her like she's made of glass and he isn't insured.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You're counting.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: One-two-three, one-two-three —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Stop counting. Watch my shoulders.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: How did you know I —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You do it on the bike. I can feel you doing it.
He watches her shoulders. And, like on the bike after the crossroads, it starts to work. He feels her lean before she leans.
They turn under the lights, slow, the band slightly out of tune, the village blurring past.
She's tall in the hat. He has to tilt his head back to look at her. He does, the whole time.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Zizzy?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Mm.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You said nobody teaches it like that any more. The old school.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …Yes.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: How do *you* know how they teach it?
She misses a step. Just one. He feels it like a bump in the road.
She thinks about telling him. The sprung floor. The squeaky board by the window. The sign. The fifteenth of September.
Her grandmother's hands on her shoulders, straightening them. *Again, chérie, again, and this time finish it.*

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Someone taught me too.
It isn't an answer. He knows. He lets it be one anyway.
The song ends. They're still holding on. A second too long. Two.
The dog in the bow tie runs between their legs and they spring apart, and the band starts a polka.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'm not doing a polka. I'll die.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'll be the first casualty of the polka.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Coward.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Survivor.
The Sorrel campsite is in the orchard itself, tents between the trees. All night there's the odd soft *thud* as an apple hits a roof, and a yelp.
Tent forty-one has, of course, the tree with the most apples.
Zizzy lies on her side of the divider. *Thud.* Pony isn't sleeping either. *Thud.*

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Zizzy?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: What.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I put the china horse on your side of the porch. Next to your boots. For luck.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Since you didn't want a snail.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's an ammonite.
A pause on the other side of the nylon. She can hear him smiling.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You kept it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …Go to sleep.
*Thud*.

She doesn't. She lies awake for an hour with the ammonite in her hand, thinking about a fortnight's summer class ten years ago, in a town he never went back to, and a teacher who said he had good feet.
Her grandmother said that. "Good feet." Her highest praise. Maybe once a year.
Lots of teachers say "good feet", Zizzy tells herself. It's a common phrase. In fencing.
*Thud.*
The rest day begins at 5:52 a.m., when an apple lands on the tent directly above Zizzy's head. There's no going back to sleep after that.
She lies there anyway, staring at the orange nylon. No route to plan. No ferry. No riddle till tomorrow.
Just a whole empty sunlit day, like a field with no road across it.
She hates it already.
Through the divider, a phone buzzes. Again. Then three times, the angry stutter of a group chat in full flow.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Nooo.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Turn it off.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I can't. It's my family. If I turn it off, they think I'm dead. If I leave it on, they think I'm ignoring them.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: There's no third option. I've looked.
Buzz. Buzz.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: My sister wants to know if I've "actually stuck at this one."
Not a joke. He reads it out flat, like the weather for somewhere he doesn't live.
Zizzy doesn't know what to say, so she says nothing. After a minute she hears him put the phone face down on the groundsheet.
By nine the campsite has scattered like dropped apples. Hammocks. The stream. Two badgers playing croquet far too seriously.
Zizzy walks. Out of the orchard, down a lane, along a stream, to a meadow so full of buttercups and clover it looks like spilled paint.
She sits alone under a willow at the water's edge.
She opens the pannier she's brought without quite meaning to, and takes out the letter.
Folded and unfolded so often it's soft as cloth. Cream paper, a solicitor's letterhead, polite the way only very bad news is.

*Dear Ms Zizzy. Further to our previous correspondence regarding the lease of the ground floor premises at 14 Mill Street, formerly held by your late grandmother… arrears of three months… we regret that unless the sum is received in full by 15th September… vacant possession…*
Vacant possession. As if the salle were something you could hold, and then just put down.
She reads it again. She knows every word. It's like pressing a bruise to see if it still hurts.
It still hurts.
The floor. Sprung beech, laid in 1971, the year her grandmother took the lease. The squeaky board by the window.
The rack of foils, some older than Zizzy, grips worn smooth by fifty years of hands.
The long mirror, cracked in one corner where an épée went astray in 1989. Her grandmother never replaced it: "It reminds them to keep their point down."
The flat upstairs, with the radio and the geraniums. Empty since March. She still has the key. Some evenings she sits in the armchair and doesn't turn the light on.
She hasn't told anyone. Not her friends. Not the club parents who keep messaging to ask when lessons start again.
She tells them "soon". She tells herself the same.
Four thousand pounds. A race. A tandem with a duck bell. In May, it seemed like a plan.
Now it looks like what it is: a girl on a bicycle, pedalling as hard as she can towards a wall.
The stream goes by. A dragonfly hovers, blue as a gas flame. She sits with the letter in her lap and, for once, isn't useful at all.
She doesn't cry. She doesn't do that. But it's a near thing, under the willow, with nobody watching.
Back at the orchard, Pony has found Bruno, the only person awake who isn't playing croquet.
Bruno is under the van, legs out, singing along to the saxophone. Pony sits on a crate nearby, turning the china horse over in his hands.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: You're hovering, strawberry.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'm sitting.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: You're sitting in a hovering way. I can hear it.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: It's a frequency. Dogs are leaving the island.
He rolls out on his board, wiping his hands, and squints up at Pony with gleeful interest.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Where's your captain?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: She went for a walk. She didn't say where.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: And you didn't follow her. Wow. Restraint. Character growth.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: She didn't want me to. She had the face.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Ooh. You know her faces now. Day five. That's fast.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's not — it's just practical. On the bike. I sit behind her all day. I've learned to read her shoulders.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Her *shoulders*.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: For *steering*.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: I love this race. Every year I think it can't get better.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Every year somebody says "her shoulders, for steering".
He sits up, takes two bottles of lemonade from a cool box, opens them with a spanner, and hands one over.
They drink in the shade of the van. The saxophone plays.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: So what's in the phone.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: What?

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: You've been looking at it like it bit you. All morning.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: I hear everything, strawberry. It's a curse.
Pony looks at the china horse. Its gold mane is chipped on one side.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: My family. They're nice. They are. I quit my degree in February. History. Second year. I just stopped going.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: In April I quit my job, at a map shop, which I loved, which is the stupid part.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: In June I quit volunteering at a kids' club, because I was too embarrassed about the other two to face anyone.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: So now whenever I start something, everybody waits for me to stop.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: And this?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: This was supposed to be the thing I finished. It has a banner.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I keep saying that like it's a joke.
Bruno doesn't say anything clever. That's the strange part. He drinks and nods slowly, taking it in.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: I quit an apprenticeship. Twice. Same garage. Went back the second time and the old boy who ran it said, "Again?"

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: I said, "Again." He said, "Fine, but this time you're finishing it, or I'm putting you in the crusher."

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Finished it. Took four years. He's dead now. I've still got his spanners.
He holds one up. Old, the chrome rubbed off the grip.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'm sorry.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Don't be. He was horrible. I loved him.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Point is, sunshine, quitting's not a personality. It's a thing you did. A few times. Doesn't mean you'll do it again.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: How do you know?

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Because you're on a mint-green tandem with a duck bell, in thirty-degree heat, in a wool hat, and you haven't got off yet.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Mate. You're the least quitty person on this island.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Wool blend.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: There he is.
Pony laughs too. It comes out wobbly. Bruno pretends not to notice, which, Pony realises, is a kindness.
Bruno is built almost entirely out of kindnesses he'd deny under oath.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Now go and find your captain. Down by the stream, in the buttercup field. Been there two hours.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Looked like a painting called *Bad News*.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: How do you —

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.expr_raw: winking, sliding back under the van
steps.text: Gossip, strawberry. I brake for it.
Giraffy intercepts him at the edge of the orchard, holding two water bottles, a paper bag and a folded blanket, with the immovable calm of a hill that has decided where the path goes.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Pony.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Hi, Giraffy, I was just —

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Lunch. Cheese, bread, apples. Two of each.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: That's very kind, but I'm not —

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Blanket. The grass by the stream is damp at the edges.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: …By the stream.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.expr_raw: holding out the water bottles, serene
steps.text: Two. Because there's two of you.
Pony looks at the bag, the blanket, the bottles. Then up at Giraffy, who gazes down from two metres with total, untroubled innocence.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Giraffy. Are you matchmaking?

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: I'm making lunch.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: For two people. By a stream. With a blanket.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: It's a very good lunch.
He puts it all in Pony's arms, pats him once on the beanie, and walks off, unhurried, towards the cook tent.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: She likes the green apples better. She won't say so.
Earlier that morning, Pony walked into Hollin for postcards and found the post office already occupied by the race organiser.
Pia is buying stamps, a great many, counting them twice. When the bell over the door rings, she jumps like a startled bird and drops half of them.

steps.speaker: pia
steps.text: Oh. Sorry. Hello. Forty-one.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Hi! Sorry. I'll get them. You've got — a lot of stamps.

steps.speaker: pia
steps.text: Postcards. To last year's riders. I send one every year. Nobody asked me to.

steps.speaker: pia
steps.text: I just like knowing where people ended up.
He hands them back. As he stands, the sword on his back knocks the postcard rack, and Pia's eyes go to it behind the big round glasses, and stay there, for a long, odd moment.

steps.speaker: pia
steps.text: That's beech.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It is. Yes. How did you —

steps.speaker: pia
steps.text: The grain. I — sorry. I should go. Riddles. Tomorrow's. Sorry.
She leaves so fast the bell is still ringing after the door shuts.
Pony stands holding a postcard of a sheep on a bicycle, with the strong, strange feeling he's just been recognised by someone he's never met.
He decides not to think about it. He's had a lot of practice this year.
She hears him before she sees him: feet swishing through long grass, a muttered "sorry" to a cow, a wooden sword clacking on a fence post.
By the time he reaches the willow, the letter is back in the pannier, and she's hugging her knees, looking at the stream as if that's all she's done all morning.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Giraffy made lunch.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: For two?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: He's very thorough.
She almost smiles. She moves over. He spreads the blanket badly; one corner folds over; she fixes it.
He unpacks the lunch and hands her the green apple without comment.
She looks at it. Then at him.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Why the green one?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Giraffy said.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …Of course he did.
They eat. The stream chatters. The dragonfly's still there, or its twin. Pony lies back, hands behind his head, beanie pulled low against the sun.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I went into the village earlier. There's a post office. It sells postcards. Hang on.
He rummages in the bag and fans out a few postcards: an apple tree, the willow throne, and a cartoon sheep on a bicycle saying GREETINGS FROM SORREL ISLE — WOOL YOU MISS ME?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I got one for you.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I thought you might want to send one. To someone.
He holds out the sheep.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You got me the pun.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's objectively the best one.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'm sending the apple tree to my mum, because she likes trees. I'll tell her I'm still on the bike. Just that. She'll understand.
He writes it there and then, on his knee, in small, neat, careful handwriting. Zizzy reads it upside down and pretends she hasn't.

then.text: *Dear Mum. Day five. Still on the bike. Learned to float (a bit). Love, P.*
*Dear Mum. Day five. Still on the bike. Learned plankton glows when it's scared. Same. Love, P.*

else.text: *Dear Mum. Day five. Still on the bike. Learned to skip stones (badly). Love, P.*

steps.text: Then he looks at her, pen held out.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Who would you send yours to?
Zizzy takes the pen and the postcard. She looks at the sheep on its bicycle for a long time.
She turns it over and writes an address she knows by heart. *14 Mill Street.* The pen stops above the name line.
There's no name to put. The flat's empty. The salle's empty.
It would land on the mat, on top of the solicitor's letters, and lie there in the dark with nobody to read it.
She holds the pen still so long that Pony stops pretending not to watch.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Zizzy?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: There's nobody there.
It just comes out. Three words. They land on the blanket between them like stones.

steps.prompt: Pony is waiting. The letter is in the pannier, an arm's length away.

options.label: Tell him. All of it: the salle, the lease, the money, why she has to win.

steps.text: She doesn't decide to. She takes the letter out of the pannier and hands it to him, the way he handed her the ammonite. As if it's obvious.
He reads it the way he reads everything, carefully, to the end, lips moving slightly on the hard words. *Arrears. Vacant possession.*
Then he looks up.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's hers. Your grandmother's.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's a salle. A fencing school. Fifty years. She taught me there from when I was four.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Then I helped her teach. Then she got ill. Then she —
The level voice goes, very briefly, somewhere else.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: The lease is in her name. Was. The rent hadn't been paid since she went into hospital. Nobody told me.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Now there's three months owing, and the landlord wants flats. If I can't pay by the fifteenth, it's gone.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: The floor, the mirror, the foils, the sign. Her flat. Everything.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Four thousand.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Four thousand.
She takes a breath. It shakes. She lets it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I haven't told anyone. Not one person.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You're the first.
Pony folds the letter along its soft old creases and hands it back. Then he sits beside her, close, his shoulder not quite touching hers.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Thank you for telling me.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Don't look at me like that.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Like what?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Like — the face. The sorry face.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'm not doing the sorry face. I'm doing the "okay, so we win" face.
She looks at him. He isn't joking. He's pushing his glasses up and frowning at the stream with ferocious concentration, the same frown he wore at the chalk line.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I came here to finish something. I didn't care if we won. I really didn't.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: But now I'd quite like to win, actually. If that's alright with you.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …That's alright with me.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Good. Then we're both here to win. Between us we've got the whole thing covered.
She laughs. Out loud, by a stream, with her face wet — when did that happen — and she doesn't care.
He doesn't say anything else. He leans, very slightly, until his shoulder touches hers. And stays.
She writes the postcard after all. To nobody. To the salle. *Day five. Still on the bike. Not alone. — Z.*

options.label: "Forget it. It's nothing." Put the postcard away.

steps.text: She puts the pen down. Postcard face down on the blanket. Picks up the green apple.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Forget it. It's nothing.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It didn't sound like nothing.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's nothing that's yours.
It comes out harder than she means. She sees it land: the flinch, the ears going back under the beanie. He looks down at *Still on the bike*, and nods.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Okay. Sorry.
That's all. He doesn't push. He never pushes. He lies back and pulls the beanie over his eyes, and leaves her her silence like a coat handed back.
She eats the apple beside him and feels worse than she did alone under the willow, which she wouldn't have thought possible.
Once, she hid a broken wrist for a week before a tournament. Her grandmother found out.
*You're the one who decides what people can carry. And you always decide they can't. That isn't strength, chérie. It's just being lonely on purpose.*
The sheep postcard goes in the pannier, next to the letter. Blank.
In the afternoon Clover finds them, following the sound of Pony reading a leaflet about the willow throne aloud, and flops onto the end of the blanket with an apple pie and three forks.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: I brought pie! Fenn's asleep in a hammock. He's been asleep since ten.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: I put a daisy chain on him. He doesn't know yet.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: He'll know.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: He'll pretend he doesn't. That's the best part.
They eat pie. Clover talks about tomorrow's Spit: the causeway's three miles long, and the tide comes in "faster than a horse can gallop". Pony looks wounded.
One year a team got stuck halfway and spent six hours in the refuge hut in the middle.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Pia's never put weather in a riddle before, though. "Bring a coat."

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Fenn read it four times. He went quiet. Quieter. You know.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Is there a forecast?

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: Sunny! It's been sunny all week. But Fenn says the swallows are flying low.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: That's a real thing. Insects fly lower in damp air before rain, so the swallows follow them —

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: See! He knows things too! You're both such *nerds*.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I'm not a nerd.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: You know exactly how many minutes it takes to get from every ferry to every checkpoint.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: You're the nerdiest of all of us.
Zizzy opens her mouth to argue. Beside her, Pony is nodding solemnly.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Don't.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I didn't say anything.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You nodded nerdily.

Late afternoon, walking back the long way, they come out on Hollin's tiny harbour: six boats, a crab shack shut for the day, and one wooden bench facing the water, built for about one and a half people.
Clover passes them going the other way with a box of ice lollies from the shop.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.expr_raw: bright, pressing one into Zizzy's hand
steps.text: Last one! You have it.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.expr_raw: bright, pressing one into Zizzy's hand
steps.text: Share! Sharing's nice! Bye!
She's gone before anyone can argue. Zizzy looks at the lolly, orange, already sweating in its wrapper. Then at the bench.
They sit. It's too small. Hip to hip, his sword knocking the armrest, her brim bumping his beanie whenever she turns her head. Neither suggests moving.
She unwraps the lolly. Bites. Holds it out sideways without looking.
He takes a careful, polite bite from the other side. She takes another. He takes another. A system develops, wordless and fair, like the tandem.
Orange drips onto her knuckle. He hands her the napkin before she asks.
The boats rock. A gull lands on the bollard in front of them and stares at the lolly with naked longing.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Don't look it in the eye.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I'm not scared of a gull.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's not about fear. It's about respect.

then.text: Down to the last bite, she holds it out to him. He pushes it gently back. She eats it.
Then she leans, just slightly, until her shoulder rests against his, and leaves it there while the tide comes in.

else.text: Down to the last bite, she holds it out to him. He shakes his head. She eats it.
They sit a while longer on the too-small bench, close because there's no choice, saying nothing. For a few minutes, the nothing isn't heavy.

steps.text: The stick says, in tiny letters, *WINNER! CLAIM ANOTHER FREE*. Pony looks at it with deep emotion and puts it in his shirt pocket.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Lucky stick.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You're going to start a museum.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I already have.

That evening Giraffy serves apple crumble to the whole campsite, the band plays one last song, and Fenn is discovered in the orchard wearing a daisy chain. He doesn't take it off. Clover glows about it all night.
Bruno does the rounds with a clipboard, checking brakes and tyres for the causeway, needling everyone. At tent forty-one he crouches by the tandem for a long time, then looks up.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Tide turns at seven-fifteen tomorrow morning. Causeway's open from about eight till half one.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: That's your window. Don't push it.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: We won't.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: And sunshine — bring the coat. Whatever coat you've got.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: I don't like that sky.
She looks up. Clear sky, blue going violet. But low on the horizon, out over the sea, a long smudge of cloud like a thumbprint on glass.
The swallows are skimming the orchard grass.
In the tent she unpacks the pannier properly for the first time all week. At the bottom, folded square, is the purple coat.
Her grandmother's, once. Taken in at the shoulders. Too warm for August. Brought anyway.
She lays it at the foot of her sleeping bag, where she'll see it first thing.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Zizzy?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Mm.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Whatever's at fourteen Mill Street.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I hope somebody's there soon.
He saw the address upside down on the blanket, the way she read his. Of course he did. He reads everything.

then.text: She lays her palm flat on the divider, just for a second, where she thinks his shoulder is.
After a moment, the nylon dips slightly on the other side. His hand against hers, through the fabric.

then.speaker: zizzy
then.text: Goodnight, Pony.

else.text: She lies still and doesn't answer. She listens to him breathe until he falls asleep, and for a long time after.

steps.text: Outside, the wind changes. The apples drop more often. *Thud. Thud.*
Far out over the sea, too far away to hear yet, the weather has started walking towards them.
The morning comes up grey.
Not storm-grey. Not yet. A flat pewter sky, a stiff south-westerly that smells of salt and something metallic.
An orchard full of riders stands about in shorts, looking at the clouds as if the clouds owe them an explanation.
Zizzy is dressed by six. Purple shirt. The coat rolled tight and strapped on top of the pannier. Hat ribbon double-knotted.
Pony emerges with the beanie on, of course, and for the first time all week looks smug about it.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Cold. It's *cold*. Do you feel that? That's beanie weather.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I've been waiting six days for this.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's sixteen degrees.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's *perfect*.
Bruno comes down the row of tents with a clipboard and none of his usual grin. He stops at forty-one.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Tide turns at seven-fifteen. Causeway opens around eight. Three miles across, refuge hut halfway.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Checkpoint five's in the hut. Stamp's inside, up the ladder. Don't ride past it.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Ferry to Hallow Key from the Spit's jetty this evening. Window closes about half one.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: And weather's coming in faster than the forecast said.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: How fast?

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Fast enough that I'd go at eight sharp and not stop to read plaques.
He looks at Pony when he says that.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I don't *always* stop.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.expr_raw: a flicker of the usual grin
steps.text: Strawberry, you stopped to read a bin yesterday.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It had a very interesting recycling chart.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Eight sharp. And if it turns, get to the hut. Don't be a hero.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Heroes are a nightmare to tow.
The causeway is just a road. That's the strange thing.
A narrow strip of tarmac, gritty with sand, running from the end of Sorrel Isle straight across a wide grey plain of mud flats and channels towards a low dark hump on the horizon: the Spit.
Tall wooden posts mark the way every fifty metres, striped with old tide marks like rings in a tree.
Halfway, on stilts, stands a little wooden box with a ladder. The refuge hut.
At high tide all of this is sea. Right now it's a road along the seabed, with the sea politely waiting on both sides.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's like riding across the seabed.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It *is* riding across the seabed. Up.
They go at eight sharp. Thirty teams at once, a ragged line of bicycles strung across the flats like beads on a thread. Fenn and Clover near the front. Clover waves. Fenn doesn't.
The first mile is fine. Fast. The road is flat as a ruler and the wind is across them, buffeting but steady. The tandem hums. "Up." "Easy." "Bump."
The second mile, the sky goes from pewter to slate.
Pony feels it first, on the back of his neck under the beanie. Then the light goes strange and yellowish.
Then the wind swings round into their faces, and the temperature drops like riding into a fridge.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Zizzy — the sky —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I see it.
Out over the sea to the south, a wall of dark grey is coming, dragging a curtain of rain. Under the curtain, the sea is white.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Up.
They push. The tandem flies. Around them other teams push too, heads down, a line of bent backs.
The hut grows on its stilts ahead, grey and solid against the darkening sky.
Then the first rain hits like a handful of thrown gravel.
In thirty seconds they're soaked. In a minute they can't see three posts ahead.
The rain comes sideways, hard and cold. The wind shoves and grabs, trying to rip the hat off her head and the bike out from under them.
And then the sea starts coming in.
Not a wave. That's what nobody tells you. Just water appearing: sheets of it, sliding across the flats from both sides, quicksilver-fast, filling the channels, spilling over the road.
The storm has pushed the tide ahead of it. The window that was meant to close at half past one is closing now.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: The road —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I KNOW. Up. UP.
An inch of water over the tarmac. Then two. The tyres throw up wings of spray.
The hut is maybe four hundred metres off, a dark box on stilts. Other teams are already scrambling up its ladder.
Then, with a crack like a branch breaking, the chain snaps.
The pedals spin loose. The tandem lurches and slews sideways. Zizzy wrenches the bars to keep them upright.
They coast to a stop in ankle-deep seawater, in the middle of the road across the bottom of the sea, with the storm coming down on top of them.
For a second neither of them moves.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: We have to leave it!

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: No.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Zizzy —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's our only bike. If we leave it, we're out.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: We push. We push it to the hut. *Push*.
He looks at her through rain-streaked glasses — at her face, set and white and furious under the dripping brim — and doesn't argue. He takes the back. She takes the front.
They push the mint-green tandem through the storm, side by side, shin-deep in rising water. Small grey waves slop across the road and break against their legs.
She counts the posts as they pass, the way she'd count steps on the strip. One. Another. Another.
The wind knocks the duck bell, and it quacks every few seconds, absurd, like a tiny brave alarm.
Pony's teeth are chattering. His mustard shirt is plastered to him. The beanie is a sodden black lump. He's shaking so hard she can see it.
Strapped to the top of her pannier, rolled tight, is the purple coat.

options.label: Stop. Untie the coat. Put it round him.

steps.text: She stops. In the middle of the flood, in the middle of the storm, she stops, which she has never once done in a race.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: What are you —
She rips the strap loose and shakes out the coat. Purple wool, heavy, old, still almost dry inside the roll.
Under the rain it smells, faintly, of geraniums and gun oil and a flat that's been empty since March.
She swings it round his shoulders and pulls it closed at his throat with both fists, and holds it, one second, so he understands she won't let go until he holds it himself.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: *Wear it*.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's yours —

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It was my grandmother's. She'd have thrown it at you. *Wear it*.
He stares at her. Rain runs down his face. Then he pulls the coat tight with one hand, the other still on the tandem.
It's too short in the arms and too narrow in the shoulders. He looks like a horse wearing a purple tent.
It's the most beautiful thing she's ever seen.
She doesn't think that. She absolutely doesn't. She grabs the bars, shouts "*Push*", and pushes.

options.label: Keep pushing. Two hundred metres. Get him to the hut.

steps.text: She thinks about the coat. About stopping. Every second they stand here, the water gets deeper.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Two hundred metres! Keep going! Stay with me!

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: With you!
They push. Her hand finds his arm on the crossbar and grips it, hard, the whole way, as if she can lend him her heat through her fingers.
She can't. But he shakes a little less anyway.
The last fifty metres are the worst. Knee-deep. The tandem wants to float, to drift out with the tide.
They drag it between them, step by step, leaning into the wind.
Then the stilts are right there, thick and tarred, and the ladder, and hands reaching down from the doorway.
Someone grabs the front wheel. Someone the back. Somehow they haul the tandem up onto the little platform.
Zizzy climbs. Pony climbs behind her. The door slams, and the storm drops to a muffled roar.
They're in.
The refuge hut is the size of a garden shed: tarred planks, a smell of rope and old salt, one small window with rain hammering it, a bench along two walls.
An oil lamp on a hook swings slightly every time the hut shudders.
And it's full. Fifteen soaking cyclists on the benches and the floor: the badgers, the weasels, a pair of otters who are delighted by all this, and a hedgehog couple who are not.
Everybody's dripping. Everybody's talking at once.
Nailed to the wall beside the lamp is a small wooden box. Inside: an ink pad and a stamp.
And a card, in Pia's bold, looping hand: *You brought your courage. Stamp here. — P.*
Checkpoint five. The fishermen's refuge hut at the midpoint of the causeway, exactly where Bruno said.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …We got here the hard way.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: "Bring your courage. Bring a coat."

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: She knew. She *knew* there'd be a storm.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: She can't have known.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Otter
steps.text: She puts checkpoint five in the hut every year, love. Just in case.

steps.speaker: extra
steps.name: Otter
steps.text: Most years folk nip up the ladder for it in the sunshine and nip down again.
Zizzy stamps the passport — a little hut on stilts, carved into a potato — with hands that won't stop shaking. Five stamps. Two to go.
There's nowhere to sit except a gap on the floor in the far corner, under the window, between a coil of rope and the wall.
They sit in it. Shoulder to shoulder. There's no other way to fit.
The storm doesn't stop. The tide doesn't turn.
The otters announce cheerfully that the next low water is a quarter past eight tonight, the causeway won't be safe till then, and in the meantime, "might as well get comfy".
So they get comfy. As comfy as you can, in a wooden box on stilts in the middle of the sea.
A flask of tea goes round. A bag of crisps. The hedgehogs fall asleep against each other.
A weasel starts a ghost story and is shouted down. The lamp swings. The rain goes on.
In the corner, Zizzy and Pony sit with their knees drawn up and their shoulders pressed together, because there's nowhere else for their shoulders to go.

then.text: He's still wearing the purple coat. He's stopped shivering. Every so often he pulls it closer and breathes in, as if the smell is something he's trying to work out.

else.text: He's stopped shivering, mostly. The flask helped. So did her shoulder, which hasn't moved from his in an hour.

steps.text: She takes her hat off — the first time all week in front of anyone but the tent — and wrings it out. Water pours from the brim.
The magenta feather is a sorry wet stripe. Beside her, Pony wrings out the beanie. It produces roughly a pint.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: The feather.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's had a long day.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's seen things.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It'll never be the same.
He laughs softly. She doesn't. But she sets the hat between her feet, leans her head back against the planks, and closes her eyes.
She lets her shoulder be heavy against his.
He holds very still. Like the kestrel. Like the sunscreen.
The storm roars. Bit by bit, the hut quietens. Snoring. A murmur from the otters. The hiss of rain.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Zizzy?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Mm.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You wouldn't leave the bike.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: No.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Most people would've.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I would've. I was going to.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I know.
A pause. The rain.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I don't leave things. I don't know how.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I just keep holding on until they're taken off me.
She opens her eyes. She's looking at the lamp, the little flame pulled sideways, then upright, sideways, then upright.
Her voice is quiet and very tired. In six days, it's the first time he's heard it without the armour.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Everything gets taken off you in the end anyway.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You just hold on until it is.

steps.prompt: In the lamplight, with her head against the planks.

options.label: Say something true.

steps.text: He takes so long that she thinks he isn't going to answer.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I don't think that's true.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You don't know.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: No. But I think some things you hold on to hold on back. That's the difference.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's not whether they get taken. It's whether they were holding you too.
She turns her head. He's very close. His glasses have steamed in the warm hut and he hasn't wiped them. She can only half see his eyes.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'm holding on. Just so you know. To this. The bike. The race. You.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I've never held on to anything for six days before. I'm not letting go.
Braver than the chalk line. Braver than the cove. He's gone pink to the ears, and he isn't looking away.

options.label: Make her laugh.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: The bike didn't get taken off you, though.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: What?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: We dragged it up a ladder. In a storm. Two otters helped.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's outside the door right now, having the worst day of its life. That bike's never been held on to so hard.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It's probably traumatised. It'll need therapy.
A pause. Then her shoulder starts to shake against his.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Stop.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It'll go to a little bike counsellor. It'll lie on a little couch.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: "Tell me about the duck."
She makes a sound into her knees — the door-creak, cracked wide open — and has to bury her face so she doesn't wake the hedgehogs.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I hate you.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: No you don't.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …No. I don't.

options.label: Ask about the sword. Tell her about the teacher.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Can I tell you about the sword?
She goes still against his shoulder.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …Yes.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: The teacher. The summer class. I was nine. We were staying with my aunt for the holidays, in a little town inland.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Mum signed me up for something to get me out of the house. I cried the first morning.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I was scared of everything at nine. Water. Dogs. Other children.
He smiles faintly.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: She didn't make me do anything. The first day I just sat by the window and watched.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: There was a board by the window that squeaked. Every time someone stepped on it, she'd say "*Again*", like the floor was telling them off.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: On the third day she put a sword in my hand and said, "You've been watching. Now show me what you saw."
Beside him, Zizzy has stopped breathing.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: She had a purple coat. Like — like yours. I used to think of her whenever I saw purple.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: On the last day she gave me the sword. She said I had good feet, and the only rule that mattered was to finish the bout.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Then we moved, and I never found the town again. I didn't even know its name. Just the squeaky board, and the coat, and "*again*".
The lamp swings. Zizzy sits perfectly still.
A squeaky board by the window. "*Again*." A purple coat.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Pony —

then.text: She turns towards him. The smallest movement. It happens without permission.
He's right there. Inches away. Lamp behind him, face half shadow, half gold, glasses still faintly fogged.
The pulse jumps in his throat above the collar she fixed. The storm, the rain, the snoring hedgehogs are suddenly nowhere near them.
He doesn't move. He's waiting, the way he always waits: for her to decide, to go first, to say "up".
So she does. She leans in. One inch. Two. Her eyes are closing —

else.text: She turns to say something. He turns at the same moment. They bump noses, not hard, and both jerk back. His glasses go crooked.
They say "sorry" at exactly the same moment, then sit very pink, staring at the opposite wall.

else.speaker: pony
else.text: That was —
