Behind them, the badgers and the weasels come flying down the switchbacks, see the bodies in the road, swerve, shout "Are you okay?" and, after a second's hesitation, keep going.
It's the last climb of the last day. They're good people, but not that good.
Zizzy leads into the last hairpin, Clover tucked on her wheel. She hears it before she sees it: a small sharp gasp as Clover unclips her left foot and the ankle folds.
Zizzy doesn't think. She brakes, twists in the saddle, throws out her right hand, and catches Clover by the shoulder of her jersey as she tips.
For one long second the two of them hang there over the gravel, held up by each other.
Then Fenn is there on the other side, and Clover is upright, white-faced, breathing hard, both feet back on the pedals.

then.speaker: clover
then.text: I'm okay. I'm okay. Thank you. Go. Go.
They go. Over the bridge. Onto the climb.
Zizzy's right hand is still shaking on the bars. It's the first thing on this bike she's caught that wasn't the wind.

else.text: Pony leads into the last hairpin, Clover tucked on his wheel. He hears it before he sees it: a gasp behind him as her left foot goes down on the loose gravel and the ankle folds.
He doesn't think either. He's off the bike before it's stopped, and reaches her as she hits the ground, and gets his arms under her before her head does.
Fenn is there a second later, white as paper under the copper hair.

else.speaker: pony
else.text: Don't move it. Fenn, hold her shoulders.

else.speaker: pony
else.text: Clover, look at me. Count with me. *Un. Deux. Trois.*
Without a word, he unstraps the wooden sword from his back, lays it along her shin, and binds it there with his yellow scarf.
Ten minutes later, she's back on the bike, the beech sword strapped to her leg, pedalling with her right foot only and laughing through tears at how ridiculous she looks.
Three teams have gone past. It doesn't matter. They climb.

then.text: Zizzy is off the tandem and running before Pony has his feet down. She drops to her knees in the gravel beside Clover.
Clover is sitting up, which is good. Her face is white and grazed down one side, and she's holding her left leg above the ankle with both hands.
She isn't crying, which is bad. Clover cries at teddy bears.

then.speaker: clover
then.text: I think I've done it properly this time.
In the ditch, Fenn is untangling himself from his bike and a bramble. His hoodie is torn at the elbow and there's blood on his palm. He doesn't look at any of it.
He looks at Clover. Only at Clover. He crawls out of the ditch on his hands and knees to get to her.

then.speaker: fenn
then.text: Clo. Clo, look at me.

then.speaker: clover
then.text: I'm looking. You've got a bramble in your hair.

then.speaker: clover
then.text: It's very dashing.
Pony kneels on her other side and, very gently, eases the cuff of her leggings up from her ankle. Under Giraffy's crossed white tape, it's swelling fast.

then.speaker: pony
then.text: It needs to be held still. Something straight.
He looks at the gravel road, the ditch, the gorse. Nothing straight anywhere.
Then he looks over his shoulder at the sword on his back.
He doesn't hesitate. That's what Zizzy will remember afterwards: he didn't hesitate at all.
He unstraps the beech sword — ten years, a washing line, the one thing he never put down — and lays it along Clover's shin.
Then he unknots the yellow scarf from the tandem's handlebars and binds the sword in place, firm and neat.

then.speaker: pony
then.text: There. It's a very good splint. It's beech.

then.speaker: clover
then.text: That's your *sword*.

then.speaker: pony
then.text: It's a stick. It was always a stick.

then.speaker: pony
then.text: The good bit was the feet.
Zizzy already has her phone out. Bruno answers on the first ring.

then.speaker: bruno
then.text: Where?

then.speaker: zizzy
then.text: Last hairpin above Hollow Bottom bridge. Clover's ankle. Fenn's hands. Nothing else.

then.speaker: bruno
then.text: Six minutes. Don't move her.
Behind his voice, the saxophone cuts off mid-note.
She hangs up. Fenn is holding Clover's hand with his good one, the bleeding one forgotten on his knee.
Without looking up, he speaks to Zizzy and Pony, plainly, the way he says everything:

then.speaker: fenn
then.text: Go.

then.speaker: zizzy
then.text: What?

then.speaker: fenn
then.text: Bruno's coming. We're out. You're not.

then.speaker: fenn
then.text: The otters are maybe four minutes ahead. The tandem climbs better than you think. Go.

then.speaker: clover
then.text: *Go!* If you stay here because of me I'll never forgive you!

then.speaker: clover
then.text: I'll buy you lollies forever, but I'll never forgive you!
Zizzy looks at Pony. Pony looks at Zizzy.
Up the hill, a long way up, the otters' jerseys flicker round a bend and are gone. Somewhere above the arch, the crowd cheers at something.
Across the gravel, the broken tandem leans against a fence post, its splint creaking in the wind, its duck bell shining.

steps.text: The old Zizzy would have gone. Said "fine", got on, and pedalled up the hill with her jaw set and her heart shut, telling herself she was being practical.
Instead she sits down in the gravel next to Clover and takes her other hand.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Six minutes. We wait for Bruno.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: Zizzy. The salle.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I know.
She does know. Every second. The otters are pulling away up the hill with four thousand pounds on their back wheel.
Fourteen Mill Street. The floor. The board by the window.
But Clover's hand is shaking in hers, and Fenn's palm is bleeding, and Pony is kneeling in the gravel holding a friend's ankle still with a sword he's carried for ten years.
Nobody here is getting left at the side of the road. Not on her race.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: She'd have stopped. She stopped for everyone.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: That's how she got hundreds of students. Not by winning.
Pony looks up at her across Clover's leg. He doesn't say anything. His face does the lamp thing, all the way up.
Bruno arrives in four minutes, not six, the sky-blue van slewing round the hairpin, saxophone off, hazards on. He's out before it stops.
He lifts Clover into the back like she weighs nothing. Fenn climbs in after her without a word, still holding her hand.
Then Bruno turns, looks at Zizzy and Pony and the tandem, and for once in nine days doesn't make a joke.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: What are you still *doing* here? *Go*.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Sit and spin. Don't stand. Go.
The climb is the hardest thing either of them has ever done.
They sit and spin. They don't stand. Every time Zizzy's legs want to stamp, she hears Bruno and doesn't. "Easy." "Easy."
The splint creaks at every stroke, a small complaining sound like an old floorboard. Like a board by a window.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: It sounds like the floor.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Don't make me laugh. I need the air.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Again.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: *Stop*.
Three hundred metres from the summit, with the arch bright against the sky and the crowd cheering, the rear stay makes a new sound.
A sharp, tired crack.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Stop.
They stop. They get off. The splint is holding, just. The tube underneath is split right through.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: One more stamp and it goes.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Then we carry it.
And they do. She lifts the handlebars. He lifts the back wheel.

They walk the mint-green tandem up the last three hundred metres of Lastlight between them, the duck bell quacking at every step, the kinked feather sticking out from her hat, and the crowd goes completely, ridiculously wild.
They cross the line together. Third. The otters won by six minutes. The weasels were second.
Nobody remembers that part. Everybody remembers the tandem.
Later, when the otters have been crowned and the champagne sprayed, and Pia has cried at the presentation, apologised for crying, and cried again, the summit empties.
The sun goes down. The light turns gold, orange, red — the same light as the chapel.

From the top of Lastlight you can see them all at once, exactly as Pia promised: Port Amble, Brackenholm, Gullrock, Sorrel, the Spit, Hallow Key, and the hill they're standing on. Seven islands in a curve on a burning sea, like the seven dots on the passport.
Seven stamps in the little blue booklet in Zizzy's hand. The last, from the finish arch, is a little stone cairn, carved by Giraffy into what he swears was his final potato of the year.
Fenn finds them there. His hand is bandaged.

Clover is down at the guesthouse with her leg up in a proper splint. She refused to give back the beech sword until Pony came to see her. So he went, and she cried on him, and gave it back, and said, "Keep the scarf on it. It suits it."
Fenn stands beside them at the edge of the summit, hands in his pockets, looking at the islands.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: I said you could have my half. If you rode with us.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You didn't win.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: Didn't say my half of what.
He takes an envelope from his hoodie pocket and holds it out. She doesn't take it. He keeps holding it. Like Pony with the sandwich.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: Two wins' worth of prize money. Never spent it. Didn't know what on.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: Thought about it in the van. Clover helped.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: A year of lessons. Paid up front. Me. Fourteen Mill Street.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: I've got a lazy back arm. Someone told me once.
Zizzy stares at him.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: Pia says I need a second thing. Clover says I need a second thing. They might be right.
She takes the envelope. Her hands aren't steady. She doesn't care.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: She'll make you hold your arm up for an hour.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: Yeah. I remember.
He nods at Pony once, one navigator to another, and walks back down the hill towards the guesthouse and the rabbit with her leg up.
And then it's just the two of them, and the cairn, and seven islands, and the sun going down.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You stopped.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You gave away your sword.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I got it back.

then.speaker: zizzy
then.text: I know. That's the point. You said it in the hut. Some things hold on back.

else.speaker: zizzy
else.text: I know. That's the point. You let go, and it came back to you.

steps.text: The wind gusts up the hill and takes her hat clean off — again.
This time neither of them lunges. It bowls away into the heather, kinked feather and all. They'll look for it in a minute.
She kisses him at the top of the world. Or he kisses her. They'll argue about it, happily, for years.
It's slow, and sure, and nobody is counting. Below them the seven islands go dark one by one, and the lights come on in all the little harbours like stars in the water.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: We finished.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: We finished.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I've never finished anything.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You have now. Again.
Bruno has, it turns out, booked them a room.
He tells them in the guesthouse doorway above Lastlight harbour, a key on a wooden fob dangling from one finger, wearing the most insufferable expression a face has ever made.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Room six. Top of the stairs. Sea view. Double bed. No divider. I asked.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: When did you book this?

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Day two, sunshine. Day *two*. The sunscreen.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: I've been sitting on this reservation for a week. Do you know how hard it is for me to keep a secret? I nearly *died*.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Thank you, Bruno.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Don't. Don't thank me.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: If you thank me I'll get emotional and I'll have to drive into the sea.
He drops the key in Zizzy's palm, ruffles Pony's beanie, and walks off down the hill to the van, whistling "Love Is in the Air", loudly, all the way to the harbour.
Room six is small and white, with a sloping ceiling and a window full of dark sea and harbour lights.
Pony lays the beech sword, still wrapped in its yellow scarf, carefully on the chair. Zizzy puts the purple hat on top of it.
The morning ferry back to Port Amble is full of sunburned, happy, limping cyclists. The brass band plays one last tune on the car deck, mostly in key.
The mint-green tandem is lashed to the rail, splint and all. Bruno has promised to buy it off the rental company and retire it somewhere nice. With geraniums.
Zizzy and Pony stand at the rail beside it.

then.text: He has the purple coat on again. She's stopped pretending she wants it back.

steps.text: She has the ammonite in her shirt pocket, and the beanie on, because he put it on her this morning as a joke and she hasn't taken it off.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Fourteen Mill Street.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Fourteen Mill Street.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Is there room for a horse? I'm good with maps. I could sweep.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I could learn to hold my arm up for an hour.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: There's a children's class on Saturdays. It's had no teacher since March.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You'd need good feet.
He stares at her. Then he beams.
September.
The sign over the old hardware shop at fourteen Mill Street has been repainted, letter for letter, in the same handwriting.

The lease is renewed for a year, paid up front with a fox's prize money and a small mountain of re-enrolment forms from club parents who had been waiting all summer for someone to say "soon" and mean it.
Zizzy lives in the flat upstairs now. The radio. The geraniums, which she has managed not to kill. The armchair, where she sits in the evenings with the light on.
Pony stays most nights. His maps are pinned up by the kitchen window. His beanie lives on the hook by the door, next to the purple coat.
The reopening was on Friday evening. Half the Long Way Round came.

Clover, on crutches, hung bunting. Fenn stood in the corner and held his back arm up for twenty minutes to prove a point. Giraffy cooked, hit his head on the doorframe four times, and each time said calmly to the doorframe, "Mind your head."
Bruno fixed the squeaky board by the window and was made to unfix it immediately. Pia gave a speech. Out loud. Without a card. It was eleven words long, and everyone cried.
Now it's Saturday morning. Early. Pale gold light through the flat's thin curtains.
Downstairs, the salle is swept and silent and waiting. The first children's class is at ten.
At five to ten, the children arrive. Eleven of them, aged seven to ten, in borrowed white jackets too big for them, solemn and terrified.
Pony stands in the middle of the sprung beech floor in a white jacket of his own, the beech sword in his hand, the yellow scarf still knotted round its hilt.
He's pushed his glasses up his nose fourteen times since nine o'clock. Zizzy counted.
One small lamb hangs back by the window, arms folded, refusing to join in. Pony glances at her. He doesn't make her do anything. He just starts.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Good morning. My name's Pony. I learned here, a long time ago, for two weeks.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: The first thing I learned is that this is a guard —
Someone steps on the board by the window. It squeaks.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: *Again*.
The children giggle. The shy lamb by the window uncrosses her arms.
Zizzy leans in the doorway in her purple hat with its kinked feather and watches him teach on her grandmother's floor.

Tucked into the crack in the mirror is a postcard of a sheep on a bicycle. On the windowsill, where a furious ten-year-old once sat: an ammonite, a hideous china horse with a gold mane, and a lolly stick that says WINNER.
She doesn't cry. She doesn't do that.
She does a little.
Pony looks up from the children, across the room, and finds her in the doorway, and his whole face lights up: a lamp, a lighthouse, the first firework.
She holds his eyes a beat longer than is comfortable.
Then she says the only thing that needs saying, quietly, the way her grandmother used to say it. Not a correction. Not a command. An invitation.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Again.
[THE END — TRUE ENDING: "The Long Way Round"]
Zizzy hesitates. One second. Two.
Then Clover shoves her. Actually shoves her, with both hands, from the gravel.

steps.speaker: clover
steps.text: GO.
They go.
Behind them, the sky-blue van slews round the hairpin with its hazards on, Bruno already leaping out.
Zizzy sees it over her shoulder and lets herself breathe. Then she faces the hill.
They sit and spin. They don't stand. The splint creaks at every stroke, like an old floorboard.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Easy.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Easy.
Halfway up, they pass the weasels, who are walking. Two-thirds of the way, a hedgehog lying in the heather waves them on.
The otters are a tiny speck far above, already near the arch.
They don't catch the otters. Nobody was ever going to catch the otters.
But a hundred metres from the top, with the crowd roaring and the arch bright against the sky, Pony leans forward and says, close to her ear:

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Can I stand? Just for the last bit? Just once?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Bruno said —

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I know what Bruno said.
She thinks about it. Nine days of sitting and spinning. The board by the window.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …Up.
They stand. Both of them. Together. The tandem leaps. The splint screams. And it holds — it holds, it *holds* — all the way across the line.
Second.
Confetti. The crowd. Pia on her crate, both hands over her mouth. Giraffy calmly holding up a hand-painted sign: GOOD FEET.
The tandem coasts to a stop past the arch, and the rear stay finally, gently, gives up with a quiet *tink*, as if it waited politely until they were done.
Zizzy gets off. Her legs don't work. She sits down in the grass in her kinked hat, laughing, really laughing, out loud, in front of everyone.
Pony sits down next to her, beanie askew, glasses steamed, laughing too.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Second. We came *second*.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: There's no prize for second.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I *finished*. I finished something. With a banner.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I've never — Zizzy, I've never —
She takes his face in both hands, firmly, so he understands she isn't letting go.
And she kisses him. Once. Short, and a little clumsy, tasting of salt, with confetti falling in both their hair.
When she pulls back, he's staring at her, stunned.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Was that — on three or after three?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: That was "up."
He kisses her back.
Somewhere nearby, Bruno is whistling "Love Is in the Air" very loudly. Clover, in the back of the van, is on the phone to Fenn's phone from three feet away, screaming.
Giraffy wanders over with two paper cups of lemonade and hands them down without a word.
He looks at the snapped stay, then at the two of them in the grass with confetti in their hair, and nods slowly.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Mostly.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Mostly.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Mostly's how most things come through.
Next morning, on the ferry back to Port Amble, they stand at the rail and talk about money, because someone has to.
There's no four thousand. There's a lease that ends on the fifteenth, and a solicitor, and a floor.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: The club parents. The ones who keep messaging.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: You said they keep asking when lessons start again.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: They do.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Then ask them for help. Not charity. Just tell them what you told me.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Let them carry a bit. They've been waiting all summer to be let.
She opens her mouth to say she can't. Then she thinks of her grandmother. *Lonely on purpose.*

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: …I'll ask.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: And I'll come. If you'll have me.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I can read a floor plan. I can carry chairs. I could do Saturdays. I'll get the train.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: The twentieth. Come on the twentieth. I'll show you the floor.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Is that a date?

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It's an observation.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'll take an observation.
The twentieth of September. A Friday. Three weeks and five days after the race.
The lease has been extended by three months. The club parents said yes before she'd finished asking.
There was a meeting in the salle, and a bake sale, and a very fierce grandmother badger who threatened the solicitor's office with her umbrella.
It isn't saved. Not yet. But it isn't lost, and there are names on a list for a Saturday class that needs a teacher.
Zizzy lives in the flat above the salle now. She moved in two weeks after the race, carrying one box and a purple coat up the narrow stairs.
The radio's on. The geraniums are still alive. Just.
Pony's train gets in at six. She meets him at the station in the kinked hat.
He's wearing the beanie, though it's still warm out, and carrying the beech sword (Clover gave it back at the summit, still wrapped in his scarf) and a bunch of slightly crushed flowers.
When he sees her on the platform, his face does the lamp thing so hard a pigeon takes off.
She shows him the floor. He stands on the board by the window, and it squeaks, and he says "Again" before she can, and she laughs so hard she has to sit down on it.
They have dinner at the little Italian place on Mill Street, where he reads her the entire history of the building off a plaque by the door. She lets him.
Then they walk back along Mill Street in the dark, slowly, the long way round, past the shut shops and the one lit window of the chip shop, to number fourteen and her grandmother's sign.
She unlocks the narrow door beside the salle, the one up to the flat.
She stands on the bottom step, which makes her taller than him even without the hat, and looks down at him.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I should — the last train's at eleven.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: It is.
Neither of them looks at a watch. She holds out her hand.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: Up?

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Up.
The next morning, Saturday, the flat smells of toast and geraniums. The radio is on low, the station she hasn't been able to stand since March. She doesn't turn it off.
Pony is at the kitchen window in her grandmother's dressing gown, far too short for him, reading the back of the marmalade jar out loud.
He missed the last train. Neither of them mentions it.
At ten, a horse in a white fencing jacket stands in the middle of a sprung beech floor in front of six nervous children and says, "Good morning. My name's Pony."
In the doorway, a zebra in a purple hat with a kinked feather watches him, and doesn't count how many times he pushes up his glasses. She doesn't need to.
It's not finished. The salle, the lease, the two of them — none of it is finished yet.
But they're still on the bike.
[THE END — GOOD ENDING: "Second Place"]

then.text: They go. Bruno's van comes round the hairpin behind them. Zizzy sees it and turns back to the hill.
They don't talk. The calls are fine. The calls are always fine. It's the silences between them that aren't.
Halfway up, Zizzy's legs remember nine days of wanting to win, and a lease, and she stands on the pedals without calling it.

then.speaker: pony
then.text: Zizzy — Bruno said —
The rear stay goes with a crack like a branch.
The tandem lurches. They stop and stand in the road and look at it: the splint hanging loose, the tube split right through, the back wheel leaning drunkenly to one side.

then.speaker: zizzy
then.text: …I didn't call it.

then.speaker: pony
then.text: No.
They push it the last two miles. Side by side. Not touching. The duck bell quacks at every bump.
The otters, the weasels, the badgers, the hedgehogs and two very old moles all pass them, kindly, one by one.
They cross the line together, ninth, walking. Pony stops just past the arch, holding the back of the broken bike, staring up at the finish banner.

then.speaker: pony
then.text: I finished.
Zizzy watches him say it. She wants to put her hand on his back. She doesn't know if she's allowed any more.

else.text: Zizzy watches from the summit, on the back bumper of Bruno's sky-blue van, the kinked feather sticking out sideways in the wind.
She sees them come up the last switchback: three riders, close together. A fox in a torn rust hoodie. A rabbit pedalling with one leg, a beech sword strapped along her shin with a yellow scarf.
And a horse on a silver bike, riding in front, upright, careful, steady, calling something over his shoulder that she can't hear but knows.
*Easy. Up. Bump.*
They cross the line together. Fourth. The crowd goes wild for the rabbit with the sword on her leg.
Fenn lifts Clover off her bike and holds her up, and she kisses him in front of everyone, and he lets her, and then — for the first time in recorded history — visibly grins.
Pony gets off the silver bike and stands under the finish banner, very still, staring up at it.

else.speaker: pony
else.text: I finished.
Then he looks round through the crowd and finds her on the back of the van. And smiles. A real one. But careful, like he's holding something he doesn't want to drop.

steps.text: The morning ferry back to Port Amble. Bright and loud, full of sunburned cyclists and the brass band.
Zizzy and Pony stand at the rail. A metre apart. The width of a harbour wall.
There's no four thousand. There's a lease ending on the fifteenth, and a floor, and nobody to teach on it.

then.text: He takes off the purple coat, folds it square, and hands it to her. She takes it. It's still warm.

then.speaker: pony
then.text: Thank you for lending it.

then.speaker: zizzy
then.text: She'd have thrown it at you.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Thank you. For the race. I finished.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I don't think I would have, with anyone else. I don't think I'd have got on the bike.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: You'd have got on.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I'd have hit a candyfloss stall.
She nearly laughs. Nearly.
The ferry bumps the quay at Port Amble. The ramp goes down.
Clover is shouting goodbye to everyone individually while Fenn carries her down the ramp. Giraffy waves one long arm. Bruno honks twice.
Pony reaches into his shirt pocket and holds out an envelope.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: Don't read it now. Read it later. Or don't.

steps.speaker: pony
steps.text: I wrote it last night. I'm better at writing things down. Pia taught me that this week.
She takes it. Their fingers touch. Neither of them moves for a moment.
Then he picks up his bag and the beech sword, goes down the ramp, and turns left, towards the station. She watches the beanie all the way to the corner.
He doesn't look back. Or he does, once, very quickly. She can't be sure. She's too far away to read his shoulders.
Giraffy is at the bottom of the ramp, coiling a rope, when she comes down alone. He doesn't ask. He falls into step beside her along the quay, unhurried, ducking under the ferry office awning.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: He read every plaque on the ferry. Out loud. To nobody.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I know.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: He kept stopping. Looking round for someone to read them to.
She stops walking. Giraffy stops too.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Apples break if you go too fast. Then you start again. Slower.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: And if it's broken already?

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Then you've got two pieces. Still an apple. Still good.
He pats her once on the kinked hat, very lightly, the way he used to pat Pony's beanie, and goes back to his rope.
She reads it that night in the armchair in the flat above the salle, with the light on.

then.text: Inside the envelope is the sheep postcard: the one she wrote *Not alone* on, by the stream, and never posted.

else.text: Inside the envelope is the sheep postcard: the blank one, from the bottom of her pannier.

steps.text: He must have taken it from the pannier on the last morning. She never noticed. He reads everything, and she never once read him.
On the back, in his small, neat, careful handwriting:

*Dear Zizzy. Day nine. I finished. Thank you. I'm still on the bike. If you ever need someone with good feet and a rubbish guard on a Saturday, I've found the town again. I won't lose it this time. — P.*
Under that, his phone number.
She sits with it for a long time. The radio plays low.
Downstairs the floor is dark, and the board by the window doesn't squeak, because nobody's standing on it.
She puts the postcard on the windowsill, next to the ammonite.
She doesn't call him. Not tonight.
But she doesn't throw it away, either.
[THE END — BITTERSWEET ENDING: "Separate Roads"]
Zizzy rides every metre of the climb standing on the pedals, as if she can stamp something out of herself through the cranks.
The silver bike takes it. It doesn't creak. It doesn't complain. Nothing on it is held together with tape.
Clover sits on her wheel. Fenn rides beside them. Nobody talks.
Halfway up, they pass the otters, who are walking. Clover gasps out "Sorry!" as they go by. Fenn says nothing.
Zizzy doesn't look at anyone. She looks at the road. At the arch at the top, bright as a rainbow. At four thousand pounds.
Her legs burn. Her chest burns. Somewhere under both, something else is burning, and she rides harder so she won't have to look at it.
They cross the line together. First.
Confetti. The crowd. The brass band. Pia on her crate, holding a small silver cup and a cheque, smiling the careful smile of someone who is happy for you and sad about something else.
Fenn steps back from the cup. Pushes Clover forward instead.

steps.speaker: fenn
steps.text: Her name first. On the plaque. She carried us.
Clover bursts into tears and kisses him in front of everyone, and the crowd goes wild, and it's a lovely moment. It really is.
Zizzy stands beside it holding a cheque for four thousand pounds, and claps.
She looks for a beanie in the crowd.
Up on the van roof. By the arch. In the queue for Giraffy's tea. At the back, where the tall ones stand.
There isn't one. Bruno told her quietly, at the bottom of the hill: Pony took the first ferry back to Port Amble, with the tandem.
He didn't watch. He'd said he wouldn't make it hard, and he didn't.
Giraffy finds her later, alone on the edge of the summit, the cheque in one hand and the ammonite in the other.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: You won.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.text: I know.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: You don't look like you know.
She doesn't answer.
Below her, seven islands in a curve on a burning sea, exactly as Pia promised. Port Amble. Brackenholm. Gullrock. Sorrel. The Spit. Hallow Key. This one.
She'd imagined seeing them for nine days. She'd imagined someone beside her, reading out their names.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: Mostly is how most things come through. Sometimes mostly isn't enough.

steps.speaker: giraffy
steps.text: That's alright. You can go back for the rest. People do.
That night there's a party for the whole field in the Lastlight harbour pub. Zizzy goes, because not going would be a speech of its own.
Everyone is kind. That's the worst of it. The otters buy her a drink and say "You were brilliant." The badgers say "Well done, love."
Nobody mentions a mint-green tandem. They don't mention it very carefully, the way people don't mention a death at a wedding.
Bruno is at the bar. He doesn't tease her. She'd give anything for him to.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: He asked me to give you something. If you won.
He puts it on the bar: the ammonite's twin. A second small grey spiral from the Gullrock cliffs, smaller than hers.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: Said he found two that day. Kept one. Said you'd know what it meant.

steps.speaker: bruno
steps.text: I don't, before you ask. First time in my life I haven't wanted to know.
She closes her hand round it. Two stones now, one in each hand. They weigh exactly the same.
Across the pub, Clover is laughing with her leg up on a stool and the silver cup in her lap, Fenn beside her with his arm along the back of her chair.
Every so often Clover glances across at Zizzy, ears halfway down, sorry and grateful at once.
Zizzy raises her glass to her. She means it. She's glad for them. She just wishes, very badly, that being glad for someone was the same as being happy.
Pia finds her at the door on her way out. At first she says nothing. Then, very quietly, she holds out a card in bold, looping handwriting.
*She'd say you finished the race. She'd ask if you finished the bout. — P.*
Zizzy puts it in her pocket with the two stones and walks down to the harbour alone.
The ferry board says the first boat back is at seven. She reads it twice, the way he would have.
September.
The lease is paid. The sign over fourteen Mill Street has been repainted, letter for letter, in her grandmother's handwriting. The squeaky board by the window still squeaks. She left it.
The first class is on a Saturday. Nine children, nervous and solemn in borrowed white jackets.
Zizzy teaches them. She's good. She was always good. She says "Again" in exactly the right voice, and the children straighten their shoulders and try again.
One of them, a small foal, has good feet and a rubbish guard. She doesn't tell him. She corrects his elbow and moves on, and doesn't look at the window.
By the window, there's a chair. She put it there before the class without thinking. Nobody sits in it.
After the children have gone, she finds a long, narrow parcel propped against the salle door in brown paper. No stamp. Hand-delivered.
Inside, a beech practice sword, the grip worn smooth by ten years of one pair of hands. A yellow scarf knotted round the hilt.
And a card. Small, neat, careful handwriting:
*It was always hers. I found the town again. You should have it back. Good feet. — P.*
Under it, an address. Not far. Two stops on the train.
Zizzy stands in the doorway of her saved salle, on her grandmother's floor, holding a sword that isn't hers, for a very long time.
Behind her, the board by the window settles, on its own, with a small creak.
Then she does what her grandmother taught her.
She doesn't hang it on the wall. She doesn't put it in a cupboard. She puts on the purple coat and the kinked hat, picks up the sword, and walks out of the door towards the station.
She doesn't know if he'll open the door. She doesn't know what she'll say if he does.
But some bouts aren't finished just because somebody won.

steps.speaker: zizzy
steps.expr_raw: quiet, to herself, at the station
steps.text: *Allez*.
[THE END — HOLLOW ENDING: "The Trophy"]
